descriptors.title: Competing factors in design
descriptors.description: Explain how people in design and technologies occupations consider competing factors including sustainability in the design of products, services and environments
descriptors.knowledge: Students can examine design and technologies occupations and factors including sustainability that impact on the design of products, services and environments (AC9TDE4K01). They have identified that designers consider multiple factors. They have not yet explained how competing factors are weighed against each other — the tension between them and how practitioners resolve it.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain how people in design and technologies occupations weigh competing factors including sustainability when designing products, services and environments, and identify examples of innovative solutions that resolve such tensions.

nodes.label: What competing factors means in design
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify that designers must weigh multiple factors that can pull in different directions, and name at least three factors that commonly compete
criteria: Names at least three factors that designers must consider
Explains at least one example where two factors conflict with each other
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot identify competing factors have no framework for design decision-making — every downstream capability (P01 investigation, P04 criteria negotiation, P03 material selection) requires reasoning through trade-offs. Without this, design decisions reduce to personal preference.

width.minimum: Name at least three factors a designer must consider (e.g. cost, sustainability, function, aesthetics, safety) and give one example where two factors pull in opposite directions
width.typical: Explain that design involves balancing competing factors that cannot all be maximised simultaneously; identify and describe how specific factors (aesthetics, function, sustainability, safety, cost) compete in a familiar product or service context
wider: Investigate how First Nations Australians considered competing factors in designing fish harvesting technologies — comparing selective harvesting techniques (fish traps, fish poisons allowing bycatch release) with high-yield non-selective methods like trawling
Investigate how Safety by Design principles (prevention, protection, proactive change) compete with other design factors such as cost and ease of use in a product or service context
Examine how engineers use biomimicry to resolve competing factors — finding a natural solution where function, sustainability and materials performance are already optimised

modes.reason: Students tend to treat factors as independent checklists rather than tensions. Multiple design contexts — each featuring a different pair of competing factors — help students see that the conflict between factors is the design problem, not just a constraint list.

nodes.label: Sustainability as a competing factor
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how sustainability considerations compete with other design priorities and identify design decisions that resolve this tension
criteria: Identifies a specific design decision where sustainability was weighed against another factor
Explains what the designer chose and why

width.minimum: Describe one product, service or environment where sustainability was weighed against another factor, and explain what design decision was made
width.typical: Explain the sustainability implications of design decisions on local, regional and global communities; describe how designers resolve tension between sustainability and other priorities in at least two contexts (e.g. materials, energy, waste)
wider: Investigate the emergence of small businesses recycling materials (e.g. plastic tags and bottle tops into prosthetics) — explaining how they resolved the competition between cost, material availability, and sustainability

Evaluate a household product designed to reduce environmental impact (e.g. a solar-powered motor, a water-harvesting system, a boardwalk through fragile wetland) — identifying which competing factors the designer prioritised and which were deprioritised

Investigate the sustainability of a community service (e.g. Clean Up Australia Day in different communities) — assessing what factors contribute to its success and what sustainability risks or failures could occur

modes.reason: Sustainability is often treated as self-evidently good — students need contexts where it genuinely competes with something valuable (cost, performance, convenience) to understand it as a trade-off that designers actively negotiate rather than a principle they simply adopt.

descriptors.title: Electrical energy transformations
descriptors.description: Explain how electrical energy can be transformed into movement, sound or light in a product or system
descriptors.knowledge: Students can describe how forces and the properties of materials affect function in a product or system (AC9TDE4K02). They understand that materials have properties that affect how products work. They have not yet connected electrical energy specifically to output transformations — movement, sound, or light — or worked with circuits as systems.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain how electrical energy is transformed into movement, sound or light in products and systems, and can identify the components needed to control these transformations.

nodes.label: Electrical energy can be transformed into different outputs
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify that electrical energy can be transformed into movement, sound or light, and give an example of each
criteria: Names at least two different outputs of electrical energy transformation
Identifies the component that performs the transformation in at least one product
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot identify that electrical energy transforms into different outputs cannot reason about which components to select or arrange in N2 — the planning and control task in N2 requires knowing what transformation is needed.

width.minimum: Identify at least two different outputs that electrical energy can be transformed into (movement, sound, light) and name a product that performs each transformation
width.typical: Explain how electrical energy is transformed into movement, sound or light across a range of products; describe what component performs the transformation in each case (e.g. motor → movement, speaker → sound, LED → light)
wider: Investigate how automated photovoltaic (solar) systems transform electrical energy to control movement in aquaculture systems — explaining how this creates opportunities for First Nations Australians in coastal northern Australia
Deconstruct a torch or buzzer to identify the components and explain how each contributes to the energy transformation — tracing the path from power source to output
Investigate how sun-tracking solar panels use electrical energy to control movement, and how this improves renewable energy production efficiency in remote communities

modes.reason: Students commonly know that electricity 'powers' things but don't think of it as a transformation — energy changing form. Multiple products each showcasing a different transformation output (motor, LED, speaker) help students build the generalisation: electricity in, different form of energy out.

nodes.label: Planning and controlling a system to produce a specific output
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how components in a circuit or system are selected and arranged to produce and control a specific output (movement, sound or light)
criteria: Identifies the components needed for a circuit producing a specific output
Explains the role of each component in the system

width.minimum: Plan the components needed for a simple circuit that produces one specific output; explain the role of each component (power source, switch, output device)
width.typical: Plan and select components for a system to perform a specific task; explain how switches, power sources and output components work together; describe how the arrangement of components controls the output (e.g. controlling movement with a switch, varying light with different resistors)
wider: Construct or model a system that controls movement, sound or light — e.g. an automaton, a pulley-based lifting system, or a circuit in a security system — explaining how each component contributes to the overall output

Investigate the properties of materials that affect a circuit's output — for example, how the reflectivity of a surface affects a light sensor in a security system — connecting material properties to system performance

modes.reason: Component selection is a reasoning task — students must work backwards from the desired output to the components needed. The reasoning chain (what output is needed? → what component produces it? → what controls it? → what powers it?) prevents students from listing components without understanding their roles.

This node integrates individual component knowledge into a working system understanding. The switch, power source and output device must be understood as a coordinated system, not separate items — the integration act is designing for a specific, controlled output.

descriptors.title: Managed food and fibre production
descriptors.description: Explain how and why food and fibre are produced in managed environments
descriptors.knowledge: Students can describe the ways of producing food and fibre (AC9TDE4K03). They understand that food and fibre come from different production systems. They have not yet explained how and why those environments are actively managed — the decisions, constraints, and sustainability practices behind production.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain how food and fibre are produced in managed environments, including soil preparation, plant and animal selection, and supply chain processes, and why these management decisions are made.

nodes.label: Why food and fibre production requires active management
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain why food and fibre production requires deliberate management decisions rather than just natural growth
criteria: Identifies at least two management decisions in food or fibre production
Explains why each decision is made — connecting it to a production goal or environmental constraint
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot explain why management decisions are made cannot sequence supply chain stages meaningfully in N2 — the 'why' of each stage (soil prep timing, harvest scheduling) requires understanding the management rationale, not just the step order.

width.minimum: Identify at least two management decisions made in a food or fibre production environment and explain why each decision is made
width.typical: Explain how soil preparation, plant selection and animal breed selection are management decisions made to match the environment; describe why specific plants or animals suit specific climates or regions — connecting environmental conditions to production outcomes
wider: Investigate how before colonisation, First Nations Australians managed food and fibre resources sustainably — including the cultivation of bunya nuts, macadamia and finger limes — and how some of these are now commercially cultivated to meet domestic and international demand

Compare tropical food production (northern Australia — higher temperature, tropical fruits) with temperate food production (cooler regions — sheep, cool-climate crops) — explaining how environment shapes management choices
Investigate and experiment with soil preparation methods (composting, mulching, nutrient cycling) and explain how each improves soil quality and production sustainability

modes.reason: Students tend to think of food production as natural rather than designed. Multiple managed environment contexts — different climates, different species, different management decisions — help students see production as a system of deliberate choices responsive to environmental constraints.

nodes.label: Supply chains — from production to retail
nodes.checkpoint: Students can sequence and explain the process of converting on-farm food or fibre products into a product suitable for retail sale
criteria: Sequences at least three stages in a food or fibre supply chain in correct order
Explains what happens at each stage

width.minimum: Identify at least three stages in a paddock-to-plate or fibre-to-garment supply chain and explain what happens at each stage
width.typical: Sequence the full supply chain for a food or fibre product — from production through processing to retail; explain what value is added at each stage and why each step is necessary; represent the chain visually (e.g. flowchart, diagram)
wider: Create a digital flowchart representing a paddock-to-plate supply chain for a locally grown product — annotating each stage with the management decisions and technologies involved
Sequence the fibre-to-garment life cycle (fibre → yarn → fabric → garment) and explain how decisions at each stage affect the sustainability and quality of the final product
Visit or virtually tour a farm and investigate how on-site decisions (breed selection, soil management, harvesting timing) affect the quality and quantity of product reaching the consumer

modes.reason: Students commonly know the end product and the raw material but cannot sequence the transformation steps. Tracing the supply chain as a connected sequence — where the output of each stage is the input of the next — makes the managed system legible as a designed process.

descriptors.title: Food characteristics and healthy eating
descriptors.description: Explain how the characteristics of foods influence selection and preparation for healthy eating
descriptors.knowledge: Students can describe the ways food can be selected and prepared for healthy eating (AC9TDE4K04). They understand that food choices affect health. They have not yet explained how specific food characteristics (nutritional value, spoilage, preparation requirements, taste) drive selection and preparation decisions.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain how the characteristics of foods — nutritional value, spoilage, preparation requirements, taste — influence selection and preparation decisions for healthy eating.

nodes.label: Food characteristics that influence selection
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and explain how food characteristics — nutritional value, availability, spoilage, taste — influence which foods are selected for healthy eating
criteria: Names at least two food characteristics
Explains how each characteristic influences whether a food is selected for healthy eating
nodes.hinge_reason: Food selection reasoning in N1 cascades directly into N2 — if students cannot identify characteristics (spoilage risk, nutritional value) as the basis for selection, they cannot connect those same characteristics to preparation decisions. The two nodes share the same conceptual structure.

width.minimum: Identify at least two food characteristics and explain how each influences whether a food is selected for a healthy meal
width.typical: Explain how nutritional value, availability, spoilage risk, preparation requirements and taste each influence food selection; apply the Australian Dietary Guidelines to plan a healthy meal or lunchbox for a specific individual — explaining selection decisions in terms of food characteristics
wider: Investigate how First Nations Australians have long selected foods based on nutritional value, seasonal availability, spoilage characteristics, and preparation requirements — exploring how this knowledge guided sustainable food choices over generations
Explore how flavour profiles (sour, salty, sweet, spicy, umami — particularly from Asian cuisines) influence food selection and preparation preferences across different cultural groups
Investigate how food service options at a local restaurant or café reflect food characteristic trade-offs — identifying how chefs balance nutrition, taste, availability and spoilage in menu design

modes.reason: Students tend to select foods based on taste preference and treat healthy eating as a rule set rather than a characteristic-based reasoning process. Multiple contexts — cultural traditions, dietary guidelines, food service — help students see food selection as applying a set of criteria to characteristics, not following a prescribed list.

nodes.label: Food characteristics that influence preparation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how food characteristics influence preparation methods and techniques
criteria: Identifies at least one food characteristic that determines how a food must be prepared
Explains the connection between the characteristic and the preparation method

width.minimum: Identify one food and explain how its characteristics (e.g. spoilage risk, texture, nutritional content) determine how it should be prepared
width.typical: Explain how different food characteristics — perishability, hygiene requirements, nutritional value, texture — determine preparation methods; apply this understanding to design a food product or meal that meets health and safety requirements
wider: Experiment with preservation techniques (pickling, fermentation, air drying, sun drying) and explain how each technique responds to specific food characteristics — connecting the preservation method to the characteristic being managed

Investigate work practices that reflect nutrition, hygiene and food safety considerations — explaining how washing produce, safe oil disposal, refrigeration of perishables, and allergen awareness each respond to a specific food characteristic
Explore the food service skills needed to prepare food for healthy eating in a restaurant or café context — identifying how preparation techniques vary with the food's characteristics

modes.reason: Students commonly follow preparation steps without connecting them to the food's characteristics. The reasoning chain — what characteristic does this food have? → what preparation risk or opportunity does that create? → what technique responds to it? — makes preparation decisions principled rather than procedural.

descriptors.title: Properties affect material use
descriptors.description: Explain how characteristics and properties of materials, systems, components, tools and equipment affect their use when producing designed solutions
descriptors.knowledge: Students can describe how forces and the properties of materials affect function in a product or system (AC9TDE4K02). They can describe material properties in relation to how products work. They have not yet explained how properties determine selection across a range of materials, systems, components, tools and equipment — or compared production approaches across different scales or cultural contexts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain how the characteristics and properties of materials, systems, components, tools and equipment affect how they are selected and used when producing designed solutions.

nodes.label: Material properties determine selection
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify properties of a material and explain how those properties determine whether it is suitable for a specific designed solution
criteria: Identifies at least two properties of a material
Explains how each property makes the material suitable or unsuitable for a specific purpose
nodes.hinge_reason: Material property reasoning in N1 is prerequisite for P01 (determining appropriate materials) and P03 (selecting and justifying material choices) — students who cannot reason from property to suitability will make unjustified material selections throughout production.

width.minimum: Identify at least two properties of a material and explain how each affects whether the material is appropriate for a specific purpose
width.typical: Describe the properties of multiple materials and explain how those properties determine their use in a designed solution — including household sustainability products, textiles, or structural applications; test or compare materials to determine which best matches the design requirements
wider: Investigate how First Nations Australians used material science knowledge to select and prepare fibres for different environmental conditions — for example, twining techniques for string and rope suited to wet, dry, freshwater and saltwater applications
Investigate the properties of fibres and design an experiment to test which fabrics are warmest — explaining how measured properties map to real-world use decisions
Compare materials used in household sustainability products (water storage, insulation, solar panels) — explaining which properties make each material appropriate for its role

modes.reason: Students typically identify properties by name without connecting them to selection decisions. Multiple design contexts — each requiring a different set of properties to be matched — build the habit of reasoning from property to suitability rather than describing properties in isolation.

nodes.label: Tools, equipment and production methods affect outcomes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how the tools, equipment and techniques used in production affect the quality and characteristics of the designed solution
criteria: Describes how at least one production tool or technique affects the outcome
Identifies at least one trade-off between different production approaches

width.minimum: Describe how at least one tool or production technique affects the quality or characteristics of a designed solution
width.typical: Compare tools, equipment and techniques across different production contexts (factory, local enterprise, handmade); explain how production scale and methods affect cost, quality and design outcomes — including environmental and social impacts
wider: Compare tools, equipment and techniques used in factories with those used by local and regional enterprises — explaining how scale, cost and design intent differ between mass production and local craft production

Compare design and production of products in Australia and a country in Asia (e.g. Indonesia) — exploring how the availability and preferred properties of materials, and the design of public structures like shelters and housing, differ by context

Describe how systems in public places (community exercise environments, water treatment plants, waste management services) are designed to benefit community life — identifying the material and system properties that make each fit for purpose

modes.reason: Students tend to see production tools as neutral — any tool does the job. Comparing production across scales (factory vs handmade) and cultural contexts (Australia vs Asia) makes visible how tool choice and technique are themselves design decisions with trade-offs for quality, cost and cultural fit.

descriptors.title: Investigate needs and processes
descriptors.description: Investigate needs or opportunities for designing, and the materials, components, tools, equipment and processes needed to create designed solutions
descriptors.knowledge: Students can explore needs or opportunities for designing, and test materials, components, tools, equipment and processes to make designed solutions (AC9TDE4P01). They have explored and tested. They have not yet investigated systematically — the shift is from exploring/testing to purposeful investigation with a view to making design decisions.
descriptors.endpoint: Students investigate needs or opportunities for designing and determine the materials, components, tools, equipment and processes required — including sustainability considerations and comparative evaluation of options.

nodes.label: Investigating a need or opportunity
nodes.checkpoint: Students can investigate a need or opportunity for designing by gathering information from multiple sources and identifying what a solution must achieve
criteria: Identifies a need or opportunity with evidence from at least two sources
States what a solution must achieve — not just what is wrong
nodes.hinge_reason: Thin investigation in N1 cascades into every downstream phase — design ideas (P02), material selection (N2, P03), and evaluation criteria (P04) all depend on having accurately characterised what the solution must achieve. An underspecified need produces solutions that solve the wrong problem.

width.minimum: Identify a need or opportunity and investigate it using at least two sources (e.g. surveying users, examining existing solutions, researching online) — summarising what a solution must achieve
width.typical: Survey users in a school or community context to identify a need; investigate existing solutions from around the world to assess suitability; identify the key requirements a designed solution must meet — including functional, social and sustainability requirements
wider: Investigate First Nations Australians' traditional fibre sources as potential commercial solutions for biodegradable string or rope — researching the materials, systems, components and processes needed to develop them commercially
Investigate small-space gardening solutions from different countries and judge their suitability for the local environment — explaining what factors determine suitability

Survey school community members about a specific need (e.g. more shade, a security system for the community garden, a community meal) — documenting needs and constraints that a designed solution must address

modes.reason: Students often investigate a single, self-identified need without testing it against actual users. Multiple investigation contexts — each with different stakeholders and information sources — build the habit of grounding needs in evidence rather than assumption.

nodes.label: Determining required materials, components and processes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can determine what materials, components, tools, equipment and processes are needed to create a designed solution — and compare options
criteria: Identifies at least two options for a material or component
Compares options using at least one criterion and justifies the selection

width.minimum: Identify at least two options for a key material or component and explain which is more appropriate for the design intention, considering at least one sustainability factor
width.typical: Test or research materials, components, tools and equipment to determine which are appropriate for the design; compare options on multiple criteria including function, cost, availability, safety and environmental impact; explain how minimising material use and managing waste affects production decisions
wider: Investigate how to minimise material use and manage waste by comparing the environmental and social impacts of alternative approaches — e.g. repurposing an old item of clothing to create a carry bag versus buying a new one
Deconstruct a product (e.g. a robotic weeder, a vacuum cleaner) to identify its components and explain the function of each — connecting component design to the product's overall purpose
Investigate complementary parts of a working system by identifying how each component's function depends on the others — explaining why changing one component would affect the whole system

modes.reason: Students typically select materials based on familiarity rather than systematic comparison. The reasoning scaffold — identify options → compare on criteria → justify selection — makes material selection a design decision rather than a default choice.

descriptors.title: Iterate and communicate designs
descriptors.description: Generate, iterate and communicate design ideas, decisions and processes using technical terms and graphical representation techniques, including using digital tools
descriptors.knowledge: Students can generate and communicate design ideas and decisions using appropriate attributions, technical terms and graphical representation techniques (AC9TDE4P02). They have generated and communicated ideas. They have not yet iterated — systematically refining designs based on evaluation — or used the full range of representation techniques including scale, symbols, digital mapping and modelling tools.
descriptors.endpoint: Students generate a range of design ideas, iterate and improve them based on evaluation, and communicate decisions and processes using technical terms and graphical representation including digital tools.

nodes.label: Generating design ideas using prior knowledge and research
nodes.checkpoint: Students can generate a range of design ideas for a product, service or environment drawing on prior knowledge, skills and research
criteria: Generates at least two meaningfully distinct design ideas
Ideas are grounded in at least one source of prior knowledge or research

width.minimum: Generate at least two distinct design ideas for the same need, drawing on prior knowledge and at least one research source
width.typical: Generate a range of design ideas for products, services or environments using prior knowledge, skills and research; represent ideas through sketches, diagrams or models; consider functional, aesthetic and sustainability dimensions across ideas
wider: Generate design ideas for an eco-friendly alternative to a non-recyclable product used in a community event — researching what sustainable alternatives exist before generating original ideas
Generate design ideas for an animal enclosure using modelling applications — iterating the layout and features based on the animal's environmental and behavioural needs

Consider the social values and ethics of clients when designing an environment — interviewing users of a space or seeking permission for designs/images from others, including respect for cultural and intellectual property

modes.reason: Students who only ever design the first thing they think of have a narrow ideation repertoire. Accumulated experience generating ideas across different product, service and environment types — each with different constraints — builds the range students can draw on when a novel design problem is encountered.

nodes.label: Representing design ideas using technical terms and graphical techniques
nodes.checkpoint: Students can represent and communicate design ideas using appropriate graphical techniques — including scale, symbols, plans, aerial views and digital tools
criteria: Uses at least one graphical convention (scale, symbols, codes, or aerial view) in a design representation
Uses technical terms to describe at least one design decision
nodes.hinge_reason: A design idea that has not been clearly represented using graphical conventions cannot be systematically analysed or modified in N3 — iteration requires a stable, readable design artifact to work from. Students who cannot represent ideas cannot iterate on them.

width.minimum: Represent at least one design idea using a labelled diagram or plan that includes at least one graphical convention (scale, symbols, or codes)
width.typical: Represent design ideas using a range of techniques — plans with scale and symbols, pictorial maps, aerial views, digital mapping tools or infographics; use appropriate technical terms when describing designs to others; select the representation technique that best communicates the design intent
wider: Use a digital modelling or mapping application to represent a design idea — for example, designing the layout and features of an animal enclosure or a community garden using digital tools
Create an infographic that presents research and design ideas to others — combining visual representation with supporting data and technical terms
Represent a design using pictorial maps and aerial views, explaining why this technique communicates the spatial relationships better than a flat plan

modes.reason: Students default to a single familiar representation technique (e.g. a labelled sketch) regardless of what the design problem needs. Different design contexts that call for different techniques — aerial view for a garden layout, diagram with symbols for a circuit, 3D model for a structure — build representation repertoire.

nodes.label: Iterating designs based on evaluation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse and modify a design idea to improve it — iterating based on sustainability, function or feedback
criteria: Identifies at least one design weakness based on a criterion
Describes a modification that addresses the identified weakness and explains why

width.minimum: Identify at least one weakness or gap in a design idea and describe a modification that addresses it
width.typical: Analyse a design idea against functional, sustainability and aesthetic criteria; modify and develop the design to improve it — documenting what changed and why; use materials, tools or equipment experimentally to refine design decisions before committing to a final approach
wider: Analyse eco-friendly alternatives to non-recyclable decorations for a community event — iterating the design to improve sustainability while maintaining function and aesthetics
Use modelling (physical or digital) to test and iterate a design idea — for example, trialling material joining techniques or component arrangements before making final choices
Replace a paper-based process with a digital equivalent (e.g. newsletters with online formats) — iterating the design to meet the same communication need more sustainably

modes.reason: Iteration integrates the evaluation from node 1 (what are the criteria?) and the representation skills from node 2 (how to document changes?) into a design improvement act. Students who generate and evaluate but don't modify have completed analysis but not design iteration — the modification is the learning.

descriptors.title: Use suitable materials and techniques
descriptors.description: Select and use suitable materials, components, tools, equipment and techniques to safely make designed solutions
descriptors.knowledge: Students can select and use materials, components, tools, equipment and techniques to safely make designed solutions (AC9TDE4P03). They have selected and used tools and materials with guidance. They have not yet matched selection decisions to design intention with explicit justification, or applied the full range of safety, hygiene and environmental considerations across material types.
descriptors.endpoint: Students select materials, components, tools, equipment and techniques that match the design intention and use them safely — applying appropriate safety, hygiene and environmental practices for the context.

nodes.label: Matching materials and techniques to the design intention
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select materials and techniques that match the design intention and explain why each choice is appropriate
criteria: Selects materials and techniques appropriate for the design intention
Explains the selection by referencing at least one relevant material property or technique characteristic
nodes.hinge_reason: Material and technique selection in N1 determines what safety practices apply in N2 — students who cannot match materials to design intention will select inappropriate tools or techniques, making N2's safety and hygiene requirements impossible to apply correctly.

width.minimum: Select a material and technique for a specific task and explain why each matches the design intention — referencing at least one material property
width.typical: Choose appropriate materials, tools, equipment and techniques for a specific design purpose; explain how the selection matches the design intention — considering function, aesthetics and sustainability; demonstrate that the selection produces the intended result
wider: Match material and joining techniques to the design intention for a textile project (e.g. a community banner, a fabric bag) — accurately cutting and joining fabric pieces as specified by the design
Select and sequence materials, tools and equipment for an electronic product — explaining how each component choice supports the circuit's intended function
Select and justify materials for a water-resistant, floating craft — explaining which material properties (density, water resistance, structural strength) determine the selection

modes.reason: Students typically select familiar materials by habit rather than matching properties to design intention. Multiple production contexts — textiles, electronics, food, structural — each requiring different property reasoning help students build the habit of justifying selection against design requirements rather than defaulting to familiarity.

nodes.label: Working safely and applying food, hygiene and environmental practices
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and apply the relevant safety, hygiene and environmental practices for their production context
criteria: Applies at least two relevant safety or hygiene practices correctly for the production context
Can explain why each practice is required

width.minimum: Identify at least two relevant safety or hygiene practices for a specific production task and apply them correctly
width.typical: Apply appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE), safe work practices, hygiene standards and environmental considerations relevant to the production context — whether food preparation, garden cultivation or construction of electronic or structural products; explain why each practice is required
wider: Apply food safety and hygiene practices in preparing a food product — including washing produce to remove residues, safe disposal of cooking oils, refrigerated storage of perishables, and managing food allergen risks
Apply safe work practices for construction tasks (e.g. protective eyewear, safe tool handling) — explaining how each practice prevents a specific risk
Identify environmental considerations when making with materials — e.g. safe disposal of chemical residues, minimising material waste, selecting materials with lower environmental impact

modes.reason: Safety and hygiene practices require consistent application across contexts, not just recognition. Students who can name practices but don't apply them consistently need deliberate practice opportunities where the habit is formed through repetition across different production contexts.

descriptors.title: Negotiate criteria and evaluate
descriptors.description: Negotiate design criteria including sustainability to evaluate design ideas, processes and solutions
descriptors.knowledge: Students can use given or co-developed design criteria including sustainability to evaluate design ideas and solutions (AC9TDE4P04). They have applied provided or jointly created criteria. They have not yet negotiated criteria — the new demand is taking ownership of developing the criteria collaboratively, including sustainability as a non-optional factor.
descriptors.endpoint: Students negotiate design criteria — including sustainability — collaboratively, and use those criteria to evaluate design ideas, processes and solutions throughout a project.

nodes.label: Negotiating design criteria collaboratively
nodes.checkpoint: Students can collaborate to develop and agree on design criteria that will be used to evaluate a designed solution — including at least one sustainability criterion
criteria: Contributes at least one criterion to a collaboratively developed set
Criteria set includes at least one sustainability criterion
Each criterion is specific enough to be applied when evaluating a solution
nodes.hinge_reason: Negotiated criteria are the prerequisite for N2 — if students have not developed criteria, they have nothing to evaluate against. N2's systematic evaluation task cannot proceed without the output of N1.

width.minimum: Collaboratively develop at least three design criteria for a specific designed solution, including at least one sustainability criterion; explain how each criterion connects to the design's purpose
width.typical: Decide on design criteria collaboratively — discussing what the solution must achieve, what sustainability means in this context (e.g. recyclable, low waste, durable), and how to make criteria specific enough to be testable; develop criteria that distinguish between requirements and preferences
wider: Develop design criteria for a beeswax wrap product — negotiating which material properties, tool requirements and sustainability factors to include as criteria, and explaining trade-offs between competing criteria

Develop criteria for a community fundraising event — including waste reduction, attendance, funds raised and consideration of how to improve future events; explain how each criterion was negotiated among the group
Include a Safety by Design criterion in the criteria set — discussing what prevention, protection or proactive change would look like as a measurable design requirement

modes.reason: Students negotiating criteria for the first time tend to produce vague or unmeasurable criteria (e.g. 'it should be good'). The criteria development scaffold — what must the solution do? → how will we know it's done? → what counts as sustainable here? — produces criteria that can actually be used for evaluation.

nodes.label: Evaluating solutions against criteria — including processes and sustainability
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate design ideas, production processes and finished solutions against negotiated criteria — including sustainability — and identify where solutions meet or fall short
criteria: Applies at least two criteria to evaluate a solution, with evidence for each
Identifies at least one area where the solution meets criteria and one where it falls short

width.minimum: Apply at least two negotiated criteria to evaluate a design idea or solution; for each criterion, state whether it is met and provide evidence
width.typical: Evaluate designed solutions, production processes and design ideas systematically against all negotiated criteria; consider benefits and costs of production processes and environmental impact; use evaluation to determine how well criteria were met and identify what could be improved
wider: Evaluate a designed solution for an animal shelter — applying criteria related to function, materials, cost and environmental impact; documenting both what was achieved and what would be changed in a future iteration

Evaluate a school or community fundraising event against multiple criteria (waste, attendance, funds, future improvement) — gathering relevant data to support each judgement rather than relying on impression

Iterate and modify a design based on evaluation — explaining exactly what changed, which criterion drove the change, and how the modification improves the solution's performance against that criterion

modes.reason: Students applying criteria for the first time treat evaluation as description — listing what they did rather than judging it against a standard. Contexts with multiple, distinct criteria each requiring different evidence (a measurement, a user response, a comparison) help students build evaluation as a multi-criteria reasoning act.

descriptors.title: Develop project plans and resources
descriptors.description: Develop project plans that include consideration of resources to individually and collaboratively make designed solutions
descriptors.knowledge: Students can sequence steps to individually and collaboratively make designed solutions (AC9TDE4P05). They have sequenced production steps. They have not yet developed full project plans that include resources, roles, timelines, milestones and digital planning tools — the shift is from step sequencing to project management.
descriptors.endpoint: Students develop project plans that sequence production steps, identify required resources, allocate roles and set milestones — using digital tools to manage and document the plan collaboratively.

nodes.label: Planning production steps and sequencing tasks
nodes.checkpoint: Students can plan and sequence the production steps needed to complete a designed solution — using digital tools to record the sequence
criteria: Sequences production steps in a logical order
Identifies at least one dependency between steps
Represents the plan using a digital tool
nodes.hinge_reason: Task sequencing in N1 is prerequisite for N2's resource allocation — you cannot specify when a resource is needed without knowing when in the sequence the task requiring it occurs. Students who cannot sequence tasks cannot produce a valid resource plan.

width.minimum: List the production steps for a design project in a logical sequence; identify at least one dependency between steps (this step must happen before that one)
width.typical: Plan production steps needed to produce a product, service or environment using digital tools — creating a flowchart, digital planner or task list that sequences tasks and includes deadlines; explain why steps must occur in a specific order
wider: Create a digital flowchart or planner that records the sequence of tasks and deadlines for a design project — including contingency steps for when a task takes longer than expected
Use a cloud-based or server-based document to record production steps and timelines — explaining the document sharing settings applied and why
Plan the production of a community meal or event, sequencing food preparation and service tasks — identifying where tasks must be done in parallel versus sequentially

modes.reason: Students who list tasks without considering sequencing constraints don't yet understand project planning as dependency management. Making dependencies explicit — this step needs the output of that step — is the key reasoning move that distinguishes planning from task listing.

nodes.label: Identifying resources and allocating roles
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the human resources, materials, tools and equipment needed for a project and specify when each is needed — allocating roles to team members
criteria: Identifies at least three resource types needed for the project
Specifies when each resource is needed relative to the production sequence
Allocates at least one role to a team member with a reason

width.minimum: Identify at least three types of resources needed for a project (human, materials, tools) and specify when each is needed in the production sequence
width.typical: Develop a project plan that identifies human resources, materials, tools and equipment with timing — setting milestones, allocating roles to team members, and specifying when shared resources need to be scheduled; include document sharing permissions when collaborating digitally
wider: Set milestones for a collaborative project — using a shared digital document or spreadsheet to list tasks, deadlines and team roles; configure document sharing permissions appropriately for the team

Plan access to a specialist resource (e.g. a wildlife expert at the planning stage, shared tools during construction) — explaining when in the production sequence this resource is needed and what constraints it creates

Develop a project plan for a habitat-building project for local animals — identifying all resource types needed at each phase and the timing constraints between resource availability and production steps

modes.reason: Resource planning integrates the task sequence from node 1 with the knowledge of what each task requires. The integration act is aligning resource availability with task timing — if a resource isn't available when needed, the plan must adapt. Students who plan tasks and resources separately have not yet integrated them.

descriptors.title: Ethics and sustainability in design
descriptors.description: analyse how people in design and technologies occupations consider ethical and sustainability factors to design and produce products, services and environments
descriptors.knowledge: Students can explain how people in design and technologies occupations consider competing factors, including sustainability, in the design of products, services and environments (AC9TDE6K01). They have identified competing factors but have not yet analysed how ethical considerations (intellectual property, cultural protocols, cross-cultural requirements) shape design decisions alongside sustainability.
descriptors.endpoint: Students analyse how people in design and technologies occupations consider ethical and sustainability factors — including intellectual property rights, First Nations Australian protocols, and cross-cultural requirements — to design and produce products, services and environments.

nodes.label: What ethical factors mean in design
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify ethical factors that designers must consider, including intellectual property, cultural protocols and the rights of communities being designed for
criteria: Names at least two ethical factors relevant to design
Explains why each factor matters for the people affected by the design
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who treat ethical factors as optional additions rather than design constraints will arrive at Node 3 unable to analyse how ethics and sustainability interact — the integration task requires ethical factors to be understood as shaping design decisions from the outset, not as a checklist appended afterward.

width.minimum: Name at least two ethical factors that a designer should consider; explain why each matters using an example
width.typical: Identify ethical factors across different design contexts — intellectual property in product design, First Nations Australian protocols in community projects, cultural consultation requirements when designing for diverse groups
wider: Research the rights and responsibilities of those working in design occupations, including First Nations Australian intellectual property rights and how these shape what a designer can and cannot do
Investigate ethical requirements when designing solutions for cultural groups — what does meaningful consultation look like?

modes.reason: Students who treat ethics as an afterthought ('add a sustainability statement at the end') rather than a design constraint ('this shapes what we can make') will produce analyses at later nodes that separate ethics from the design process. Seeing ethics across multiple design contexts helps students understand that ethical factors are integral, not optional.

nodes.label: Sustainability as a design constraint
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse how sustainability considerations constrain and shape design decisions about materials, processes and outcomes
criteria: Identifies at least one sustainability consideration in a design scenario
Explains how the sustainability factor affects design choices
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who understand sustainability only in one dimension (e.g. recycling) will produce partial analyses at Node 3 — the integration task requires sustainability to be understood as operating across lifecycle stages and across cultural and economic contexts simultaneously.

width.minimum: Identify at least one sustainability consideration in a given design scenario; explain how it affects what the designer can choose
width.typical: Analyse sustainability across the design lifecycle — material sourcing, production processes, product lifespan, end-of-life disposal; explain trade-offs between sustainability and other factors like cost or performance
wider: Investigate how traditional technologies from Asian countries are sustained or transformed in response to environmental or economic change
Research offshore manufacturing implications — how does moving production to another country affect sustainability and ethical considerations?

modes.reason: Sustainability as a design constraint operates differently across product lifecycle stages (material sourcing, production, disposal) and across cultural and economic contexts (e.g. offshore manufacturing). Students who see sustainability only in one dimension (e.g. recycling) will produce partial analyses. Breadth across lifecycle stages and contexts builds the multi-dimensional understanding needed for Node 3.

nodes.label: Analysing ethics and sustainability together in design occupations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse how people in design occupations weigh ethical and sustainability factors together when designing and producing products, services or environments
criteria: Analyses how at least one ethical and one sustainability factor together shape a design decision
Does not treat ethics and sustainability as separate checklists — explains how they interact

width.minimum: Given a design scenario, analyse how at least one ethical and one sustainability factor together influence the design decisions made
width.typical: Compare how ethical and sustainability factors are balanced in design across Australia and a country in Asia; identify where factors compete and how designers navigate the tension
wider: Compare design and production across additional industries or country pairs beyond the core Australia-Asia examples
Investigate enterprise opportunities that arise when ethical and sustainable design creates a competitive advantage

modes.reason: This node requires students to bring ethical factors (Node 1) and sustainability constraints (Node 2) together into a single analysis. Students who have treated them as separate checklists produce analyses where the two factors coexist but don't interact. The integration task reveals whether students understand that ethical and sustainability considerations can reinforce, trade off against, or constrain each other.

descriptors.title: Innovation for preferred futures
descriptors.description: analyse the impact of innovation and the development of technologies on designed solutions for global preferred futures
descriptors.knowledge: Students can explain how people in design and technologies occupations consider competing factors, including sustainability, in the design of products, services and environments (AC9TDE6K01). They have identified factors but have not yet analysed the impact of innovation or emerging technologies on designed solutions, or considered how design contributes to global preferred futures.
descriptors.endpoint: Students analyse the impact of innovation and the development of technologies — including traditional, contemporary and emerging technologies — on designed solutions, and evaluate how these contribute to global preferred futures.

nodes.label: What innovation means in design
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain what innovation means in a design context and identify factors that drive or enable innovation
criteria: Defines innovation in a design context (not just 'something new')
Identifies at least two factors that drive innovation
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who define innovation only as 'something new and digital' will not recognise traditional or adaptive technologies as innovation at Node 2, producing incomplete comparisons and a distorted analysis of impact at Node 3.

width.minimum: Define innovation in design terms; identify at least two factors that drive innovation (e.g. new materials, societal change, environmental need, technology development)
width.typical: Explain how multiple factors interact to drive innovation — developing novel ideas, responding quickly to change, creating a point of differentiation, adding value for society, reducing costs or improving efficiency
wider: Limited width — the concept of innovation is a single insight. The genuine breadth comes from seeing innovation applied across different technology types and contexts at later nodes.

modes.reason: Understanding what drives innovation requires accumulating a range of examples — students who only see technology-driven innovation will miss social, environmental and economic drivers. Building a repertoire of innovation examples across driver types is the prior condition for analysing technology types at Node 2.

nodes.label: Traditional, contemporary and emerging technologies
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare traditional, contemporary and emerging technologies and analyse how each contributes to designed solutions
criteria: Gives a correct example of each technology type (traditional, contemporary, emerging)
Does not equate innovation with only new or digital technology
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who equate innovation with only new or digital technology cannot meaningfully analyse impact at Node 3 — they will evaluate only emerging technologies and dismiss traditional approaches, producing an incomplete account of how innovation contributes to preferred futures.

width.minimum: Give one example each of a traditional, contemporary and emerging technology; explain how each solves a design problem
width.typical: Compare traditional and contemporary approaches to the same design challenge (e.g. First Nations bushfire management vs IoT sensors and drones); analyse how emerging technologies respond to changing social, environmental or economic needs
wider: Investigate how traditional technologies from a country in Asia are sustained or transformed in response to environmental or economic change
Research how biomimicry (e.g. Velcro inspired by burrs) or new materials drive innovation in manufactured products

modes.reason: Students who see 'innovation' as only meaning new/digital technology will dismiss traditional technologies and miss the insight that innovation includes adapting, sustaining and reinterpreting existing approaches. Seeing traditional, contemporary and emerging technologies side by side across different cultural contexts resolves this misconception.

nodes.label: Impact on preferred futures
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse how innovation and technology development impact designed solutions and evaluate their contribution to global preferred futures
criteria: Identifies at least one positive and one negative impact of a design innovation
Connects the impact to what kind of future it contributes to

width.minimum: Given a design innovation, analyse at least one positive and one negative impact; explain what 'preferred future' it contributes to or undermines
width.typical: Analyse the impact of innovation across social, environmental and economic dimensions; evaluate competing design factors — for example, how house design or waste management practices in a country in Asia balance sustainability with livability
wider: Investigate design factors for First Nations Australian communities in remote areas — how does innovation need to account for place, culture and access?
Compare how the same innovation (e.g. smart farming, renewable energy) impacts differently in urban vs remote vs developing contexts

modes.reason: Analysing impact on preferred futures requires students to draw on both the innovation concept (Node 1) and the technology type comparison (Node 2) to make an evaluative judgement. Students who have only accumulated examples without building analytical tools will describe impacts without evaluating what kind of future they contribute to.

descriptors.title: Force, motion and energy control
descriptors.description: analyse how force, motion and energy are used to manipulate and control engineered systems
descriptors.knowledge: Students can explain how electrical energy can be transformed into movement, sound or light in a product or system (AC9TDE6K02). They understand energy transformation in simple systems but have not yet analysed how force, motion and energy are applied together to manipulate and control more complex engineered systems.
descriptors.endpoint: Students analyse how force, motion and energy are used to manipulate and control engineered systems, including testing components for structural or functional performance and calculating system outputs.

nodes.label: Force, motion and energy in systems
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify how force, motion and energy each contribute to the function of an engineered system
criteria: Identifies force, motion and energy as distinct contributions in a system
Does not conflate force with energy or motion with force
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who conflate force, motion and energy will produce system analyses at Node 3 that describe components without accurately tracing the input-process-output chain — the control analysis depends on treating the three concepts as distinct contributions.

width.minimum: Given an engineered system, identify which components involve force, motion or energy; explain what each contributes to the system's function
width.typical: Analyse how force, motion and energy work together in multiple systems — for example, how wind turbines transform wind energy to electricity, how control systems use energy to produce motion
wider: Investigate renewable energy systems in remote communities such as wind turbines on Torres Strait Islands — how force, motion and energy are harnessed for sustainable power
Investigate a control system for a real need, such as the Phillip Island penguin weighbridge — how energy, sensors and motion work together

modes.reason: Students who cannot distinguish between force, motion and energy as separate concepts in a system will conflate them when analysing more complex systems. Seeing the three concepts operating distinctly across different engineered systems builds the discrimination needed for analysis at later nodes.

nodes.label: Testing and prototyping
nodes.checkpoint: Students can experiment with components to test structural or functional performance and use prototyping to test ideas
criteria: Tests at least one component for a specific property
Records the result and explains what it means for the design

width.minimum: Test at least one component for a specific property (e.g. structural strength, battery durability); record the result and explain what it means for the design
width.typical: Test multiple components to select the most appropriate for a design; use prototyping (including rapid prototyping tools like 3D printers) to test functionality before committing to production
wider: Limited width — testing and prototyping are processes applied the same way regardless of system. The breadth comes from the variety of systems being tested, which is captured at Nodes 1 and 3.

modes.reason: Testing and prototyping require methodical practice — setting up fair tests, recording results accurately, drawing valid conclusions from test data. The skill doesn't vary across contexts but students need repeated practice to develop the discipline of systematic testing.

nodes.label: Controlling engineered systems
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse how force, motion and energy are controlled in engineered systems, including calculating outputs and identifying failure points
criteria: Explains how a system is controlled — what inputs produce what outputs
Identifies at least one point where the system could fail

width.minimum: Given an engineered system, explain how it is controlled — what inputs produce what outputs; identify at least one point where the system could fail
width.typical: Analyse control in multiple systems; calculate system outputs (e.g. speed, brightness, volume); determine when the system might fail based on component limits
wider: Explore control systems using microcontrollers or object-based programming to control motion — how does software control physical systems?
Investigate how batteries, motors or other components determine system limits and failure points across different applications

modes.reason: Analysing control in engineered systems requires students to trace the input-process-output chain and identify failure points at each stage. Scaffolding the reasoning structure (what is the input? → what process transforms it? → what is the output? → where could this break?) prevents students from describing system function without identifying control points or failure modes.

This node integrates force, motion and energy concepts from Node 1 with testing/prototyping methods from Node 2 into a complete system analysis. Students who have not connected the three concepts and their measurement will produce system analyses that describe components without explaining how they interact to achieve control.

descriptors.title: Sustainable managed production
descriptors.description: analyse how food and fibre are produced in managed environments and how these can become sustainable
descriptors.knowledge: Students can explain how and why food and fibre are produced in managed environments (AC9TDE6K03). They understand that production is managed but have not yet analysed the techniques used to increase production ethically and sustainably, or compared production methods across contexts including First Nations and Asian approaches.
descriptors.endpoint: Students analyse how food and fibre are produced in managed environments — including ethical and sustainable techniques for increasing production — and evaluate how these methods can become more sustainable across different production contexts.

nodes.label: How managed environments work
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how managed environments for food and fibre production control growing conditions to increase yield and quality
criteria: Identifies at least two managed factors in a production environment
Explains how managing each factor affects yield or quality
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who know only one or two management variables cannot compare or evaluate approaches at Node 2 — the ethical/sustainable technique analysis requires a working repertoire of managed factors to assess what each technique achieves.

width.minimum: Identify at least two factors that are managed in a food or fibre production environment (e.g. soil, water, nutrients, pest control); explain how managing each affects production
width.typical: Analyse how physical and chemical characteristics of soil affect plant growth; investigate different management strategies (e.g. grazing vs supplementary feeding for animals) and their effects on quality
wider: Investigate how traditional First Nations Australian food and fibre sources offer sustainability benefits such as water conservation or resilience
Compare land and water management methods between Australian and Asian production contexts, including smart farm technologies such as robotics and GPS

modes.reason: Understanding how managed environments work requires encountering a range of management variables — soil chemistry, water, nutrients, pest control, animal nutrition. Students who only know one or two management strategies cannot later compare or evaluate approaches. Building the repertoire of managed factors is the prior condition for Node 2's analysis.

nodes.label: Ethical and sustainable techniques
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse the ethical and sustainable techniques used in food and fibre production and evaluate their effectiveness
criteria: Identifies at least one ethical and one sustainable technique
Does not conflate ethical with sustainable — explains what each specifically achieves
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who conflate ethical and sustainable techniques, or treat sustainability as a single checkbox, will produce superficial evaluations at Node 3 — proposing improvements requires accurately distinguishing what each technique achieves and why.

width.minimum: Identify at least one ethical and one sustainable technique used in food or fibre production; explain what each achieves
width.typical: Compare ethical and sustainable techniques across production systems — animal welfare practices, organic vs conventional methods, water management strategies; analyse trade-offs between sustainability and productivity
wider: Investigate the relationship between animal nutrition strategies and product quality across different production systems
Research how food and fibre production contributes to Australia's food security and economy, including trade with Asian countries

modes.reason: Students who cannot distinguish ethical from sustainable techniques (or who treat sustainability as a single checkbox) will produce superficial analyses. Seeing multiple ethical and sustainable techniques across different production contexts — animal welfare, organic farming, water management, cultural practices — builds the discrimination needed for genuine analysis.

nodes.label: Making production more sustainable
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate how food and fibre production methods can become more sustainable and propose improvements based on analysis
criteria: Identifies at least one way a production method could become more sustainable
Explains why the proposed change improves sustainability

width.minimum: Given a production method, identify at least one way it could become more sustainable; explain why the change would improve sustainability
width.typical: Evaluate sustainability across the production lifecycle — sourcing, growing, harvesting, processing, transport; propose and justify improvements that balance sustainability with economic viability
wider: Investigate traditional First Nations Australian food sources for potential species that offer sustainability benefits in contemporary production
Compare how different countries approach sustainable production of the same commodity — what works in one context and why it may not transfer directly

modes.reason: Evaluating how production can become more sustainable requires students to reason from evidence: identify current practice → identify the sustainability problem → propose a change → explain why the change improves sustainability → consider trade-offs with productivity. Students who propose changes without this reasoning chain produce aspirational statements rather than evaluations.

This node integrates managed environment knowledge (Node 1) and ethical/sustainable technique analysis (Node 2) into a forward-looking evaluation. Students must apply both to propose improvements that are both technically feasible and genuinely more sustainable.

descriptors.title: Food properties and presentation
descriptors.description: analyse how properties of foods determine preparation and presentation techniques when designing solutions for healthy eating
descriptors.knowledge: Students can explain how the characteristics of foods influence selection and preparation for healthy eating (AC9TDE6K04). They understand that food characteristics matter for healthy eating but have not yet analysed how specific food properties (sensory properties, nutrient retention) determine preparation and presentation techniques.
descriptors.endpoint: Students analyse how the properties of foods — including sensory properties (flavour, texture, appearance, aroma) and nutrient value — determine the selection of preparation and presentation techniques when designing solutions for healthy eating.

nodes.label: Food properties that matter
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the sensory properties and nutritional properties of foods that influence how they should be prepared
criteria: Names at least two sensory properties of food
Explains how at least one property is affected by preparation
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who know only two sensory properties will not be able to explain preparation trade-offs at Node 2 — selecting between techniques requires understanding how multiple properties respond differently to different methods, and that sensory and nutritional properties can pull in opposite directions.

width.minimum: Name at least two sensory properties (e.g. flavour, texture, appearance, aroma) and explain how each is affected by preparation
width.typical: Distinguish between sensory properties and nutritional properties; explain how preparation techniques can enhance one while diminishing another (e.g. roasting improves flavour but may reduce nutrient value)
wider: Investigate how First Nations Australians prepare foods to improve edibility — for example, leaching toxins from seeds or using specific cooking methods that preserve nutritional value
Compare how the same food's properties are valued differently across cultures — what one culture considers desirable texture or flavour may differ from another

modes.reason: Food properties must be accumulated across types before students can reason about how preparation affects them. Students who only know two sensory properties will not be able to explain preparation trade-offs at Node 2. More food examples with different property profiles build the repertoire needed.

nodes.label: How preparation techniques affect properties
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse how different preparation techniques impact sensory properties and nutrient retention
criteria: Explains how a preparation technique changes at least one sensory property
Identifies whether the technique improves or reduces nutrient value
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who treat preparation techniques as generic 'cooking methods' rather than deliberate choices that transform specific properties will not be able to select and justify techniques at Node 3 — design for healthy eating requires knowing how each technique affects both sensory appeal and nutrient value.

width.minimum: Given a preparation technique, explain how it changes at least one sensory property and its effect on nutrient value
width.typical: Compare multiple techniques (e.g. stir-frying vs steaming vs boiling) and analyse how each affects flavour, texture, appearance and nutrient retention differently; explain how a recipe can be modified to enhance health benefits
wider: Analyse food preparation techniques from Asian cultures (e.g. stir-frying, steaming, poaching) and their impact on nutrient retention compared to Western techniques
Investigate how traditional wood selection for roasting and smoking complements flavour in First Nations cooking

modes.reason: Students who think of preparation techniques as simply 'cooking methods' rather than as deliberate choices that transform food properties will not be able to design solutions for healthy eating at Node 3. Seeing how different techniques produce different outcomes across multiple food types and cultural traditions builds the analytical framework needed.

nodes.label: Designing for healthy eating
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select and justify preparation and presentation techniques based on food properties when designing solutions for healthy eating
criteria: Selects a preparation technique appropriate for the food and the health objective
Justifies the choice by referencing specific food properties

width.minimum: Given a healthy eating goal, select a preparation technique and explain why it suits the food's properties and the health objective
width.typical: Design a food solution that balances sensory appeal with nutritional goals; justify technique and presentation choices by referencing specific food properties; modify an existing recipe to improve its health benefits while maintaining appeal
wider: Compare food design solutions across cultures — how different traditions balance health, flavour and presentation using different techniques and different foods
Design a food solution for a specific dietary requirement and evaluate how preparation techniques support both the nutritional need and sensory experience

modes.reason: Designing for healthy eating requires students to draw on food property knowledge (Node 1) and preparation technique analysis (Node 2) simultaneously — selecting a technique requires knowing both what it does to sensory properties and how it affects nutrient retention. Students who have learned these separately often design without considering both dimensions.

descriptors.title: Combining materials and systems
descriptors.description: analyse how characteristics and properties of materials, systems, components, tools and equipment can be combined to create designed solutions
descriptors.knowledge: Students can explain how characteristics and properties of materials, systems, components, tools and equipment affect their use when producing designed solutions (AC9TDE6K05). They understand that properties affect use but have not yet analysed how different materials and systems are combined, or how the interaction between properties determines what a designed solution can achieve.
descriptors.endpoint: Students analyse how the characteristics and properties of materials, systems, components, tools and equipment can be combined to create designed solutions, including testing and selecting the most appropriate options for a given purpose.

nodes.label: Properties that determine use
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the characteristics and properties of materials, components and equipment that determine their suitability for different design purposes
criteria: Names at least two properties of a material or component
Explains how each property affects suitability for the design purpose
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who know properties of only two materials will not have enough comparison points to analyse combinations at Node 2 — explaining why a combination works requires understanding how the properties of each material complement or constrain the others.

width.minimum: Given a material or component, name at least two properties and explain how each affects its suitability for a specific design purpose
width.typical: Compare properties across a range of materials and components; explain safe work practices for specific equipment; identify which properties matter most for a given design challenge
wider: Investigate the significance of hafting in First Nations Australian traditional toolkits — how the properties of resin, cord and stone combine for function
Research advanced materials such as carbon fibre reinforced polymers and explain what properties make them suitable for high-performance applications

modes.reason: Property identification requires building a repertoire of material-property-purpose relationships before students can analyse combinations. Students who only know properties of two materials will not have enough comparison points to explain why particular combinations work. More material examples with different property profiles is what helps here.

nodes.label: How combining creates new possibilities
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse how combining different materials, systems and components creates designed solutions that individual components could not achieve alone
criteria: Identifies at least two components combined in a designed solution
Explains what the combination achieves that individual components could not
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who treat materials as isolated choices cannot make evidence-based selection justifications at Node 3 — the testing and selection task requires understanding that choosing one component constrains or enables the choice of others.

width.minimum: Given a designed solution, identify at least two components that are combined; explain what the combination achieves that neither component could alone
width.typical: Analyse how materials, tools and processes are combined across a range of technologies contexts (e.g. architecture, textiles, electronics); explain how the choice of one component constrains or enables the choice of others
wider: Investigate how First Nations Australians combine material properties in traditional toolkit construction — how do the properties of each material complement the others?
Compare material choices for the same design challenge across different contexts — architecture, medicine, sport — and analyse why different combinations are optimal

modes.reason: Students who think of materials as isolated choices ('pick the strongest one') rather than as combinations where properties interact will produce designs where components conflict rather than complement.
